newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus court backs deputies in Lukashenko row.
newsitem.headline: Belarus court backs deputies in Lukashenko row.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko's parliamentary enemies eased ahead in a battle for power in Belarus on Monday, when the constitutional court effectively asserted their right to stop him increasing his powers.
But Lukashenko's press service immediately dismissed the decision, saying the court had broken the law.

The court voted 8-3 that deputies would have the final say on results of a November 24 referendum, where Lukashenko will seek to amend the constitution and restart his five-year term -- extending it by more than two years without elections.
"The parliament would in fact be excluded from the constitutional process," if the voters' decision was binding, the court's ruling said.

Lukashenko will also seek the right to create an upper house partly appointed by him, and name all court judges, half the constitutional court and half the members of the commission which monitors and runs elections.
The court's decision means that even if voters back Lukashenko, parliament will in theory be able to block the move as the referendum results would not be constitutionally binding.

Deputies would in theory also be able to abolish the presidency altogether, as the issue will be raised on November 24, but political analysts say it is unlikely such a radical move would be carried to its conclusion.
Alexander Plaskovitski, head of the judicial deparment of Lukashenko's administration, told Reuters the president might ignore the court anyway.
"The constitutional court has found a cunning and confusing way of stopping the referendum being mandatory. Thus the result of the referendum will simply be a bit of good advice," he said.
"But if the president decides the verdict contradicts the constitution, he has the right not to carry it out," he added.

Lukashenko's press service said in a statement read out on state television that the court had "crudely violated the referendum law," adding: "The constitutional court has refused the people their right to take a decision".
Lukashenko, accused by his political opponents of trying to build a dictatorship, has ignored 17 rulings by the court that his decrees were unconstitutional.
The communist deputy speaker of parliament, Vasily Novikov, said deputies would discuss the decision at Tuesday's session.
The court stepped back from declaring the referendum unconstitutional -- a move which Lukashenko had said would lead him to dissolve parliament.
Lukashenko has been battling a majority of deputies over the referendum and many other issues since he won a landslide victory on a platform of fighting crime in July 1994.
Since then he has suspended trade unions, closed newspapers and frozen the country's privatisation programme.
The 44-year-old president has drawn criticism from the West for his increasingly authoritarian rule and lending bodies have suspended credits pending faster reforms.

Lukashenko became the former Soviet republic's first post-Soviet president in July 1994, winning a landslide victory on a platform of fighting corruption and pressing for a union of some sort with neighbouring Russia.
